prompt.context: Our client is an upscale restaurant in TianJin, serving government officials and high-level business customers. Its monthly revenue is 1.2 million Yuan. The CEO recently hired McKinsey to help them increase profits. As China's economy is booming, the upscale dining market is growing at 20% every year. Customers for high-end dining are generally price insensitive. All competitors are earning money. Competitors' price and value proposition are similar. Variable costs across the industry is 50% of revenue. Assume no fixed costs. On weekdays, there is always a line for individual rooms. As a result, the restaurant has to turn away half of its customers due to capacity constraints.
prompt.question: The CEO has hired McKinsey to help increase profits. What are the reasons for low profits and what solutions would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: What is the seating arrangement — how many rooms and tables does the restaurant have?
clarifying_info.a: The restaurant has two types of seating: Individual Rooms (20 tables) and Big Rooms (20 tables).

clarifying_info.q: What are the occupancy, price per person, and party size for each seating type across weekday/weekend and lunch/dinner?
clarifying_info.a: Individual Rooms (20 tables): Weekday Lunch — occupancy 80%, price 150 Yuan/person, party size 4. Weekday Dinner — occupancy 100%, price 300 Yuan/person, party size 6. Weekend Lunch — occupancy 30%, price 100 Yuan/person, party size 4. Weekend Dinner — occupancy 50%, price 200 Yuan/person, party size 6. Big Rooms (20 tables): Weekday Lunch — occupancy 20%, price 100 Yuan/person, party size 4. Weekday Dinner — occupancy 30%, price 200 Yuan/person, party size 4. Weekend Lunch — occupancy 30%, price 100 Yuan/person, party size 4. Weekend Dinner — occupancy 30%, price 200 Yuan/person, party size 4.

clarifying_info.q: Why is demand for individual rooms so high relative to big rooms?
clarifying_info.a: Government officials and business customers prefer individual rooms to big rooms because of their requirement for privacy. Currently the client is not meeting customer demand.

framework: Diagnose the revenue gap: understand seating types, occupancy, pricing, and where demand exceeds capacity
Identify the root cause: individual rooms are over-subscribed (turning away 50% of weekday customers) while big rooms are underutilized
Evaluate revenue-upside levers: (1) raise prices in capacity-constrained segments, (2) convert underutilized big-room tables into individual rooms
Quantify each solution: calculate incremental profit from price increase and calculate total cost (capital + opportunity) of renovation
Recommend the optimal path and sequence

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of low profits given the restaurant context?
questions.guidance: The restaurant is capacity-constrained in individual rooms on weekdays — it turns away half its customers. Meanwhile big rooms have very low occupancy (20-30%). The target customers (government officials, business customers) demand privacy, so they prefer individual rooms. The low overall utilization of big rooms is the structural mismatch. The restaurant is leaving significant revenue on the table.

questions.prompt: Market research shows that raising weekday individual room prices by 33% will cause a 10% customer loss. How will this change profitability?
questions.guidance: Analyze weekday lunch and weekday dinner separately. For lunch, demand is not fully constrained so the 10% volume loss applies. For dinner, underlying demand is 200% of capacity, so raising price will NOT reduce volume — guests turned away will simply fill the slots. Calculate incremental profit for both and sum them.

math.setup: Variable costs are 50% of revenue, so profit margin is 50%. Analyze lunch and dinner separately for weekday individual rooms (20 tables).
steps: WEEKDAY LUNCH (Individual Rooms): Previous customers = 4 persons/table x 20 tables x 80% occupancy = 64 persons. New customers = 64 x (1 - 10%) = 57.6 ≈ 58 persons. Previous revenue = 64 x 150 = 9,600 Yuan. New revenue = 58 x 200 = 11,600 Yuan (price raised 33%: 150 x 1.33 = 200). Previous profit = 9,600 x 50% = 4,800 Yuan. New profit = 11,600 x 50% = 5,800 Yuan. Incremental profit (lunch) = 5,800 - 4,800 = 1,000 Yuan/day.

WEEKDAY DINNER (Individual Rooms): Underlying demand is 200% of capacity, so volume stays at 100% occupancy. Previous customers = 6 persons/table x 20 tables x 100% = 120 persons. New customers = 120 (unchanged). Previous revenue = 120 x 300 = 36,000 Yuan. New revenue = 120 x 400 = 48,000 Yuan (price raised 33%: 300 x 1.33 = 400). Previous profit = 36,000 x 50% = 18,000 Yuan. New profit = 48,000 x 50% = 24,000 Yuan. Incremental profit (dinner) = 24,000 - 18,000 = 6,000 Yuan/day.
math.answer: Daily incremental profit from the price increase = 7,000 Yuan/day.

questions.prompt: A second solution is converting half of the big room tables (10 tables) into 5 individual rooms. Renovation takes 2 weeks and requires a complete shutdown. Decoration cost is 100,000 Yuan. What is the total cost of this project?
questions.guidance: Total cost = capital investment + opportunity cost. The opportunity cost is the profit foregone during the 2-week shutdown. An observant candidate will use the monthly revenue figure (1.2M Yuan/month) rather than reconstructing revenue from the detailed table, since 2 weeks ≈ half a month. Profit margin is 50%, so monthly profit ≈ 600K Yuan, and 2 weeks ≈ 300K Yuan opportunity cost.

math.setup: Capital investment = 100,000 Yuan. Opportunity cost = profits lost during 2-week shutdown. Monthly revenue = 1,200,000 Yuan; monthly profit at 50% margin = 600,000 Yuan. 2 weeks = approximately half a month.
steps: Opportunity cost = 1,200,000 x 50% x (2/4 weeks per month) = 600,000 x 0.5 = 300,000 Yuan (approximately).
Total cost = capital investment + opportunity cost = 100,000 + 300,000 = 400,000 Yuan.
math.answer: Total cost of the renovation project = approximately 400,000 Yuan.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential solutions to increase profits for the restaurant?

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Raise prices in capacity-constrained individual room segments (weekday lunch and dinner)
Implement dynamic or surge pricing on peak days/times
Introduce premium add-ons or tasting menus to increase revenue per cover

categories.name: Capacity Reallocation
ideas: Convert underutilized big room tables into individual rooms
Optimize table turnover rates during peak periods
Add a reservation-only system to reduce walk-away rate

categories.name: Demand Management
ideas: Encourage off-peak demand with discounts or promotions for weekends/lunch
Create loyalty or membership programs for recurring government/business clients
Introduce a waiting list or advance booking fee to monetize overflow demand

categories.name: Cost Optimization
ideas: Negotiate better terms with food suppliers given growing scale
Reduce waste through better demand forecasting
Streamline kitchen operations to lower variable costs below 50%

recommendation: In the short term, raise weekday individual room prices by 33%, generating approximately 7,000 Yuan incremental profit per weekday
In the medium term, convert half of big room tables into individual rooms at a total cost of ~400,000 Yuan to permanently address the capacity constraint and capture the unmet demand
risks: The renovation requires a full 2-week shutdown which creates customer disruption and foregone revenue (~300K Yuan opportunity cost)
If economic conditions slow, price-insensitive customers may become more sensitive
Big room conversion may limit flexibility if future customer mix shifts toward larger parties
next_steps: Implement the price increase immediately as it requires no investment and yields positive returns from day one
Commission detailed renovation planning to minimize shutdown duration
Monitor customer response to price increase over 4-6 weeks before committing to renovation
Model the post-renovation revenue uplift from the new individual rooms to confirm payback period
